..
Thursday: Moisture pivoting around an area of low pressure 
tracking into Oregon will bring periods of light precipitation 
to the Inland NW. We are seeing trace amounts of snow in the 
upper river valleys of the Cascades where temperatures are 
hovering near freezing. More persistent snow will impact the 
Wenatchee Mountains and badger mountain area of the Waterville 
Plateau into the morning hours where a combination of upslope, 
northeast flow and increasing lapse rates will coincide. Tough 
to determine how much snow has fallen so far but cams from 
Mission Ridge and Blewett Pass indicate persistent snow with 
reports of winter driving conditions on the pass. Light snow has
also been observed near Waterville. Winter weather advisories 
will remain in effect above 3000 feet until Thursday morning 
with precipitation expected to slowly taper off through the day.
Clouds and areas of light rain will be slower to clear out of 
the lower Idaho Panhandle and southeastern WA as the parent low 
migrates across Oregon and to the east. 

Friday: High pressure briefly amplifies along the WA coast and a 
robust shortwave drops southward down the Continental Divide. 
This system will clip the Idaho Panhandle bringing a reinforcing
shot of cooler air and band of snow. Several of the 
deterministic models indicate the potential for a tenth or more 
of QPF which would equate to a few inches of snow for the 
Central Panhandle Mountains and Lookout Pass. There are some 
differences how far west this wave reaches in the ensembles 
which is causing the NBM to wash out the QPF to near zero. 
Pattern recognition would suggest these systems have 
overachieved in the past and forecast has been adjusted to 
reflect snow for Friday afternoon into the evening. REFS has a 
50% chance for at least an inch of snow at Lookout Pass. Central
WA and majority of Eastern WA will remain dry with passing 
clouds. 

Saturday-Sunday: Another deep low pressure system will swing to 
the WA Coast slinging a shortwave into the Inland NW. Saturday 
will be dry for much of the region through the afternoon. By the
evening, clouds and precipitation will be on the increase 
across the Cascades with a cool occluding front tracking west to
east through the remainder of the Inland NW overnight into 
Sunday. The region will be on the cool side of the jet with 
850mb temperatures anywhere from -1C in the southern Columbia 
Basin to -4C near the Canadian border. Consequently, the first 
round of wintry precipitation is expected to move through the 
Inland NW. Aside from the lowest elevations in the lower Basin 
and L-C Valley, there is an 80% chance for snow to fall across 
the lowlands but the probabilities for receiving an inch 
drastically lower to 20% or lower for all areas south of Hwy 2 
and even the northern valleys as QPF amounts taper off. This is 
from the NBM. So it looks favorable for most communities to 
experience snow falling but there is considerable uncertainty if
this lowlands will receive an inch. Deterministic models do 
indicate higher QPF with upwards of a tenth to three tenths with
this band which would certainty support an inch of snow at a 
10:1 ratio. One of the greater challenges will be how cold do 
the surface temperatures become before the clouds move in. If 
they remain closer to 34F, this will lower potential 
accumulations. Soil temperatures are also still running in the 
upper 30s that could result in melting. I feel the potential for
light accumulations will be elevation dependent with locations 
below 2000 feet having lower probabilities and those above 2000 
feet higher and amounts will continue to increase with future 
updates. 

Monday-Thursday: The remnants of the offshore low ejects inland 
Monday with continued chance for rain and snow showers. This 
activity could become more convective in nature as the remnants 
of the 500mb cold pool slides through the region. The forecast 
becomes a lot more uncertain heading into the holiday week with 
a myriad of different scenarios. There is a lot of agreement of 
another robust low settling into the Eastern Pacific. What is 
less certain is exactly where this system will set up. If 
further offshore, the region could experience a period of 
ridging and quiet weather with fog as the main concern. If 
closer to the coast, the weather has the potential to remain 
active with additional snow in the Cascades and northern 
mountains early in the week. Of greater concern is when does 
the system come inland and does this coincide with late week 
holiday travel. The potential is there but confidence is very 
low with details. If you are planning to travel across the 
passes, we urge you to monitor the forecast for updates on 
potential snow impacts.
